messages.subject: Hierarchical zero-inflated gamma (working example)
parts:
I've been translating a few ongoing data analysis projects into Stan code, mostly with success. The most important for me right now has been a hierarchical zero-inflated gamma problem. This a "hurdle" model, in which a bernoulli GLM produces zeros/nonzeros, and then a gamma GLM produces the nonzero values, using varying effects correlated with those in the bernoulli process.

Originally, I had written the sampler myself in raw R code. It was very slow, but I knew what it was doing at least. Just before Stan version 1.0 was released, I had managed to get JAGS to do it all quite reliably. But JAGS was taking a long time to converge and then producing highly autocorrelated output. Stan has been amazing, in comparison. I could hardly believe the traceplots. Stan produces the same inferences as my JAGS code does, but with 8 hour runs (no thinning needed) instead of 30 hour runs (with massive thinning).

I'm confident that there are places where the speed and precision in my model code could be improved. But not even trying to do so, it beats JAGS handily. Many thanks for the effort behind Stan.

Below is the framework for the zero-inflated model, abstracted to a simulated data example. I've put the model code inline for convenience of reading, and then attached the full R script. The only real trick needed here is to replace observed zeros with some positive real, so vectorized calculations on gamma density don't throw errors ("No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?"). 

    data {
        int<lower=0> N;                 // number of cases
        int<lower=1> J;                 // number of clusters
        real<lower=0> y[N];             // observed outcome
        int<lower=0,upper=1> iszero[N]; // indicates a zero outcome
        int<lower=1> id[N];             // cluster number for each case
        cov_matrix[2] Omega;            // diagonal prior
    }
    parameters {
        vector[2] mu;                   // means of varying effects
        cov_matrix[2] Sigma;            // var-cov matrix for varying effects
        vector[2] alpha[J];             // varying effects for each cluster
        real theta;                     // log scale
    }
    model {
        real pi;                        // probability of zero GLM
        real mugamma;                   // mean of gamma GLM
        Sigma ~ inv_wishart( 3 , Omega );
        mu[1] ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
        mu[2] ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
        theta ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
        for (j in 1:J) alpha[j] ~ multi_normal( mu , Sigma );
        for (n in 1:N) {
            pi <- inv_logit( alpha[ id[n] , 1 ] );
            mugamma <- exp( alpha[ id[n] , 2 ] );
            lp__ <- lp__ + if_else( iszero[n] , log(pi) , log1m(pi) + gamma_log( y[n] , mugamma*exp(theta) , exp(theta) ) );
        }
    }
    generated quantities {
        real dev;                       // deviance of each set of samples
        real pi;                        // temp for computing dev
        real mugamma;                   // temp for computing dev
        real rho;                       // correlation btw varying intercepts
        real sd[2];                     // sd of varying intercepts
        dev <- 0;                       // not sure need to init to zero
        for ( n in 1:N ) {
            pi <- inv_logit( alpha[ id[n] , 1 ] );
            mugamma <- exp( alpha[ id[n] , 2 ] );
            dev <- dev + (-2) * if_else( iszero[n] , log(pi) , log1m(pi) + gamma_log( y[n] , mugamma*exp(theta) , exp(theta) ) );
        }
        for( k in 1:2 ) sd[k] <- sqrt( Sigma[k,k] );
        rho <- Sigma[1,2] / sqrt( Sigma[1,1] * Sigma[2,2] );
    }

>> thinning needed) instead of 30 hour runs (with massive thinning).

That still seems like a long time!

In running in R and comparing speeds, is
everyone making sure to reset R's compiler
to use optimization level -O3?
Stan is MUCH faster with -O3 than with R's
default -O2 level (as will be anything else compiled
from source through R, so it's a good idea
even if you don't use Stan).

See the R getting started guide for instructions
on how to do it.

It's also important to make sure you're using
a version of JAGS compiled with -O3, by the way.
>> I'm confident that there are places where the speed and precision in my model code could be improved
>> Many thanks for the effort behind Stan.

You're welcome. We're very happy to see people making
good use of it.

See below.

>> Below is the framework for the zero-inflated model, abstracted to a simulated data example. I've put the model code
>> inline for convenience of reading, and then attached the full R script. The only real trick needed here is to replace
>> observed zeros with some positive real, so vectorized calculations on gamma density don't throw errors ("No acceptably
>> small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?").

Is the problem on the branch of the if-else you're using?
The problem with if-else is that unlike a proper ternary
operator (cond ? valT : valF) which only evaluates the
expression valT if the condition is true and valF if
the condition is false, the if-else always evaluates
both because it's compiled to a function.

I'm going to write proper conditionals into Stan soon.

The code looks great. I'm so happy people are figuring out
how to code complex (in Stan coding terms) models like this.

>> |
>> data {
>> int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
>> int<lower=1> J; // number of clusters
>> real<lower=0> y[N]; // observed outcome
>> int<lower=0,upper=1> iszero[N]; // indicates a zero outcome
>> int<lower=1> id[N]; // cluster number for each case
>> cov_matrix[2] Omega; // diagonal prior
>> }
>> parameters {
>> vector[2] mu; // means of varying effects
>> cov_matrix[2] Sigma; // var-cov matrix for varying effects
>> vector[2] alpha[J]; // varying effects for each cluster
>> real theta; // log scale
>> }
>> model {
>> real pi; // probability of zero GLM
>> real mugamma; // mean of gamma GLM
>> Sigma ~ inv_wishart( 3 , Omega );
>> mu[1] ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
>> mu[2] ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
>> theta ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
>> for (j in 1:J) alpha[j] ~ multi_normal( mu , Sigma );
>> for (n in 1:N) {
>> pi <- inv_logit( alpha[ id[n] , 1 ] );
>> mugamma <- exp( alpha[ id[n] , 2 ] );
>> lp__ <- lp__ + if_else( iszero[n] , log(pi) , log1m(pi) + gamma_log( y[n] , mugamma*exp(theta) ,
>> exp(theta) ) );

Once we've vectorized all the distributions, it'll be
easy to speed this up another factor of 2 or 3. It's
our top priority right now.

I would've written your model as follows:

real exp_theta;

real mugamma; // mean of gamma GLM
Sigma ~ inv_wishart( 3 , Omega );
mu ~ normal(0,100); // vectorized

theta ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
for (j in 1:J) alpha[j] ~ multi_normal( mu , Sigma );
exp_theta <- exp(theta);
for (n in 1:N) {
iszero[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha[id[n],1]);
mugamma <- exp( alpha[ id[n] , 2 ] );

for (i in 1:(1 - iszero[n]))
y[n] ~ gamma(mugamma * exp_theta, exp_theta) );
}

I pulled exp(theta) out of the loop, which will save
both memory and time.

The replacement of your pi terms with bernoulli_logit is
based on the definition:

bernoulli_logit_log(u) = log(bernoulli(inv_logit(u)))

This should be faster, use less memory, and be more
arithmetically stable.

I'm sorry to say we don't have a proper conditional yet,
but I'm going to add one pretty soon. Until then,
I've adopted Marcus Brubaker's hack using a for loop
above. This relies on the fact that if the range is
(1:0) the loop executes zero times and if the range
is (1:1) the loop executes exactly once. Given that
you coded iszero[n] as being binary (this is why I like
type constraints and type declarations!), the above will
work.

I'm curious how much faster it'd be if you made the
above changes.

We're (and by that I mean Daniel Lee) are also working hard
on vectorizing the various distributions. It's a bit of
a hard slog on the C++ side, but he's been making good headway.

Is it common to have log-scale parameters for gamma?
If so, that'd probably be worth adding as a parameterization
because exp() transforms are very hard on arithmetic
precision and computation.

Really we should just build in the zero-inflated Poisson.

>> cov_matrix[2] Omega; // diagonal prior

Why not use (y[n] == 0) instead of iszero[n]? iszero[n]
would be only the tiniest fraction faster.

Another thing one can do in these mixture modeling
with known assignments is to change the data shape.
For instance, build two arrays, y_zero with the
zero entries and y_nonzero with the nonzero entries.
Then you don't need to branch in the code at all.

And often (not here as you have other item-level
effects) you can gather up sufficient statistics
like number of zero outcomes and simplify some
calculations.

- Bob

Yes, feel free to quote me on the blog. And thanks for all the coding suggestions. I'll try them out and see how much the speed can improve at the margin.

A little more detail: The data are 20 years of human foraging returns from a subsistence hunting population in Paraguay (the Ache), comprising about 15k hunts in total (Hill & Kintigh. 2009. Current Anthropology 50:369-377). Observed values are kilograms of meat returned to camp. The more complex models contain a 147-by-9 matrix of varying effects (147 unique hunters), as well as imputation of missing values. For the JAGS/Stan comparison, the machine I ran both on was a 3.09GHz i5, OS X 10.8, 12GB RAM. Stan was compiled with -O3, but JAGS wasn't.

In the future, I should be getting similar data for about a dozen other foraging populations, so will want to scale this up to a meta-analytic level, with partial pooling across societies. So the improved efficiency from Stan will be a huge help going forward as well.

On the horizon, I have a harder project I'd like to port into Stan, involving cumulative multi-normal likelihoods. I wrote my own sampler, using likelihoods from pmvnorm in the mvtnorm package, but it mixes very slowly, once all the varying effects are included. Is there a clever way to get the same likelihoods in Stan yet? If not, once you have a guide prepared for how to compile in new distributions, I can probably use that to hack mvtnorm's pmvnorm into Stan.

Hey, can I quote you on the blog?
